quiz.q: What are the two shapes of Option<T>?
quiz.explain: Option<T> is Some(value) when there's a value, or None when there isn't. It's Rust's safe replacement for null.

quiz.q: What are the two shapes of Result<T, E>?
quiz.explain: Result<T, E> is Ok(value) on success or Err(error) on failure, carrying a real error value describing what went wrong.

quiz.q: Why does `match` on an Option or Result help catch bugs?
options: It's exhaustive — the compiler refuses to build unless every case (including None/Err) is handled
It automatically logs errors to the console
It converts Option into Result for you
quiz.explain: match requires every variant to be handled. Forget the None or Err arm and the compiler rejects the code as non-exhaustive, catching a whole class of 'forgot to check' bugs.

quiz.q: What happens when you call `.unwrap()` on a `None` or an `Err`?
quiz.explain: unwrap() panics (crashes the program) on None/Err. It's convenient in tests and quick scripts, risky in real code a user runs.

quiz.q: What must the closure passed to `.and_then()` return?
options: A plain value of any type
Another Option (or Result) — the same kind of container
Nothing — and_then discards the return value
quiz.explain: and_then chains another fallible step, so its closure must itself return an Option/Result. If it returns a bare value, you wanted .map() instead.

quiz.q: You have `let price: Option<i32> = Some(10);` and want `Option<i32>` back with the value doubled. Which combinator?
quiz.explain: .map() transforms the value inside Some/Ok with a plain (infallible) closure and re-wraps the result automatically.

options: Converts a Result into an Option, discarding the error
Converts an Option into a Result, using `err` as the Err value when it's None
Panics if the Option is None
Filters an Option based on a predicate
quiz.explain: .ok_or(err) turns Option<T> into Result<T, E>: Some(v) becomes Ok(v), and None becomes Err(err).

options: There is no difference, they're aliases
unwrap_or takes a ready-made value; unwrap_or_else takes a closure that only runs (computing the fallback) on the failure path
unwrap_or only works on Result, unwrap_or_else only works on Option
quiz.explain: unwrap_or's argument is always evaluated eagerly; unwrap_or_else's closure is only called when there's actually a None/Err, useful when computing the fallback is expensive.

Converts the Result into an Option
Keeps Some(n) only if the predicate is true; otherwise turns it into None
Runs the closure on every character of the string
quiz.explain: .filter() on Option keeps Some(value) only when the predicate returns true for the inner value; otherwise it becomes None.

flashcards.front: What is Option<T> used for, versus Result<T, E>?
flashcards.back: Option<T> models 'a value might simply be absent' (no reason needed). Result<T, E> models 'an operation might fail, and here's why' — it carries an error value.

flashcards.front: Why is unwrap() risky in real code?
flashcards.back: It panics (crashes the whole program) on the first None/Err it sees. Fine for tests and quick scripts; risky in anything a user runs, since there's no chance to recover or show a nice message.

flashcards.front: What does .map() do on an Option/Result?
flashcards.back: Transforms the value inside Some/Ok using a plain (non-fallible) closure, leaving None/Err untouched. The result is automatically re-wrapped in Some/Ok.

flashcards.front: What does .and_then() do, and how is it different from .map()?
flashcards.back: and_then chains another fallible step: its closure must itself return an Option/Result (not a bare value). Unlike map, it doesn't re-wrap — this avoids ending up with Option<Option<T>>.

flashcards.front: What does .ok_or(err) do, and what does .ok() do?
flashcards.back: .ok_or(err) converts Option -> Result, using err as the Err when it's None. .ok() goes the other way, converting Result -> Option and discarding the error value.

flashcards.front: unwrap_or(default) vs unwrap_or_else(|| ...) — when would you pick each?
flashcards.back: unwrap_or(default) when the fallback is cheap and ready-made. unwrap_or_else(|| ...) when computing the fallback is expensive or needs the error value — its closure only runs on the failure path.

flashcards.front: What does .filter() do on an Option?
flashcards.back: Keeps Some(value) only if a predicate returns true for the inner value; otherwise turns it into None. Useful for adding a validity check after parsing or looking something up.

flashcards.front: Why does `match` on Option/Result prevent a class of bugs that null checks don't?
flashcards.back: match is exhaustive — the compiler refuses to compile unless every variant (Some/None or Ok/Err) is handled, so you literally cannot forget to check the failure case.
